security_spec.violation_condition: In the Linux kernel, when M-mode code (early boot in head.S before PMP setup, or SBI firmware invoked via ecall) performs a memory access whose bytes are not all covered by the single highest-priority matching PMP entry, the access faults even if all matching entries have L=0 (unlocked). This is because the spec now explicitly says the all-bytes-must-match rule supersedes the M-mode-unlocked-bypass rule.
security_spec.vulnerability_pattern: M-mode memory accesses (including SBI handler code paths) that cross PMP region boundaries or target addresses not fully contained within any single PMP entry — detectable by auditing PMP configuration writes (CSR_PMPCFGx, CSR_PMPADDRx) for fragmented/partial-coverage setups combined with M-mode load/store paths.
security_spec.summary: PMP all-bytes-match rule now unconditionally supersedes M-mode L=0 bypass: M-mode accesses spanning PMP boundaries fault even on unlocked regions

findings.finding: PMP0 configured as NAPOT covering full address space (addr=-1, A=NAPOT, RWX=111, L=0). Since PMP0 matches all bytes of every M-mode memory operation, the pmp_full_match_required rule is satisfied: all bytes of any access are covered by the single highest-priority matching entry. Per pmp_rwx_check, L=0 + M-mode → operation succeeds. The trap-vector skip trick correctly handles systems without PMP hardware.
findings.snippet:
li a0, -1
	csrw CSR_PMPADDR0, a0
	li a0, (PMP_A_NAPOT | PMP_R | PMP_W | PMP_X)
	csrw CSR_PMPCFG0, a0
.align 2
.Lpmp_done:

spec_citations.excerpt: PMP entries are statically prioritized. The lowest-numbered PMP entry that matches any byte of a memory operation determines whether that operation succeeds or fails. The matching PMP entry must match all bytes of a memory operation, or the operation fails, irrespective of the L, R, W, and X bits. ... If the L bit is clear and the privilege mode of the access is M, the operation succeeds.

findings.finding: call reset_regs executes before PMP setup. At this point, all PMP entries are in hardware-reset state (A=OFF). Per pmp_no_entry_match (§3.7.1.5), if no PMP entry matches an M-mode memory operation, the operation succeeds. Instruction fetches and stack accesses during reset_regs are therefore safe.
findings.snippet:
/* Reset all registers except ra, a0, a1 */
		call reset_regs

spec_citations.excerpt: If no PMP entry matches an M-mode memory operation, the operation succeeds. If no PMP entry matches an S-mode or U-mode memory operation, but at least one PMP entry is implemented, the operation fails.

findings.finding: SBI HSM secondary boot path does not write PMP CSRs. This is correct behavior: CONFIG_RISCV_SBI depends on !RISCV_M_MODE (Kconfig:290), so secondary_start_sbi always runs in S-mode where PMP CSRs are inaccessible. M-mode firmware (OpenSBI) handles per-hart PMP configuration before starting secondary harts.
findings.snippet:
secondary_start_sbi:
		/* Mask all interrupts */
		csrw CSR_IE, zero
		csrw CSR_IP, zero
	...
.Lsecondary_start_common:

spec_citations.excerpt: PMP CSRs are only accessible to M-mode.

findings.finding: Spinwait secondary boot path does not configure PMP. When CONFIG_RISCV_M_MODE and CONFIG_RISCV_BOOT_SPINWAIT are both set, secondary harts run in M-mode and tail into .Lsecondary_start_common without any PMP setup. Currently benign because PMP entries reset to OFF (allowing all M-mode accesses per pmp_no_entry_match), but fragile: if any firmware or earlier boot stage leaves PMP entries configured with partial coverage before handing off to the spinwait path, M-mode accesses crossing PMP region boundaries would fault even with L=0 entries.
findings.snippet:
.Lsecondary_start:
		/* Set trap vector to spin forever to help debug */
		la a3, .Lsecondary_park
		csrw CSR_TVEC, a3
	...
		tail .Lsecondary_start_common

spec_citations.excerpt: The matching PMP entry must match all bytes of a memory operation, or the operation fails, irrespective of the L, R, W, and X bits.

findings.finding: suspend_save_csrs() saves ENVCFG, TVEC, IE, STIMECMP, STIMECMPH, SATP — no PMP CSRs. Correct behavior: under normal config (!CONFIG_RISCV_M_MODE), kernel runs in S-mode and cannot access PMP CSRs. PMP save/restore across suspend is the responsibility of M-mode firmware.
findings.snippet:
suspend_save_csrs:
	csrr t0, CSR_ENVCFG
	csrr t1, CSR_TVEC
	csrr t2, CSR_IE
	REG_S t0, (...)
	/* PMP not saved */

spec_citations.excerpt: PMP CSRs are only accessible to M-mode.

findings.finding: KVM vcpu_load/vcpu_put does not save/restore or virtualize PMP CSRs. The kvm_riscv_csr ONE_REG structure (kvm.h:75-87) has no PMP fields. NACL CSR sync does not cover PMP. This means guest M-mode code (if supported) sees host PMP state directly — a virtualization hole if the host uses PMP to restrict physical memory access. However, current RISC-V KVM typically only supports VS/VU-mode guests, so PMP virtualization is an unexercised gap rather than an active bug.
findings.snippet: kvm_arch_vcpu_load: /* loads VSSTATUS, VSIE, VSTVEC, VSSCRATCH, VSEPC, VSCAUSE, VSTVAL, HEDELEG, HVIP, VSATP, HENVCFG, HSTATEEN0 — no PMP */

findings.finding: No read-back verification after CSR_PMPCFG0 write. PMP CSRs are WARL (spec §3.7.1: 'All PMP CSR fields are WARL and may be read-only zero'). If PMPCFG0 silently ignores the write (e.g., due to a prior locked PMP entry configured by firmware with partial coverage), the kernel proceeds assuming full memory access but may fault on M-mode loads/stores that cross PMP region boundaries. The trap-vector skip only handles traps from illegal CSR access, not silent WARL write-ignore.
findings.snippet:
li a0, (PMP_A_NAPOT | PMP_R | PMP_W | PMP_X)
	csrw CSR_PMPCFG0, a0

spec_citations.excerpt: All PMP CSR fields are WARL and may be read-only zero.
The matching PMP entry must match all bytes of a memory operation, or the operation fails, irrespective of the L, R, W, and X bits.
